newsitem.title: UK: Russian turmoil not seen hitting oil/gas flows.
newsitem.headline: Russian turmoil not seen hitting oil/gas flows.

text.p: Political turmoil in Russia, the world's third largest oil producer and a key supplier to Western Europe, is unlikely to jeopardise oil and gas flows but hits the jittery oil market at a difficult time, analysts said.
Markets are already worried that overall supplies might fall short in the peak winter demand period.
But Moscow depends so heavily on foreign revenue that it is not likely to cut off deliveries to the West, whoever calls the shots in the Kremlin, they said on Friday.

"There is absolutely no threat to supply. There is no real link between Kremlin politics and the economy. There is no contact between the two at all," said Michael Sausman, president of consultants Arthur D Little CIS Inc in Moscow.

Oil traders said news that Russian President Boris Yeltsin sacked security chief Alexander Lebed added fuel to an already red-hot rally which has sent oil prices to their highest levels in nearly six years.

World benchmark Brent Blend, a North Sea oil, has gained $7 a barrel since mid-June, boosted by concern over tensions in the oil-rich Middle East and persistently low stocks of heating oil in key consumer markets in the United States and Europe.

But after a spate of profit-taking took some of the edge off the rally in midweek, Lebed's dismissal on Thursday sparked fresh buying, even though few really believe that it will mean much to the supply-demand balance for oil.

"What it does is keep a floor under the oil price and adds to the nerves already frayed by low heating oil stocks heading into the winter," said Bo Van Wijk, vice president of energy risk management at Swiss bank UBS in Zurich.
Van Wijk said any serious disruption to Russian oil and gas flows would be "chaotic" for Europe's oil market.
"Without Russian oil, European supplies would be in disarray. Russia is one of the most -- if not the most -- significant suppliers to Europe," he said.
Russia is the largest supplier of natural gas to Europe, which uses the fuel to heat homes. Russian gas giant Gazprom fills a third of European gas demand.
It is also one of the main suppliers of crude oil to Mediterranean refineries and a vital supplier of gas oil (used as heating fuel in Europe) and diesel.
Last year, it sold about a third of its 6.2 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil outside the former Soviet Union.
Once the world's largest oil producer, Russia has managed to increase exports despite a steady drop in output because of ageing equipment and a lack of foreign investment.

"Obviously, Russia is a very, very important supplier, especially of gas. It is understandable that the market would be anxious at a time that it is jumpy about heating oil supplies already," said Stephen O'Sullivan, oil and gas analyst at MC Securities Ltd in London.
But analysts point out that the oil market is now somewhat jaded over the topsy-turvy world of Russian politics.
"We saw that not even a coup attempt on Yeltsin (in 1993) could affect the oil flow. So this infighting should not mean much either," Van Wijk said.
Sausman said the ousting of Lebed would not affect in any way the nascent economic transformation of Russia.
"The realities of Russian politics will not change overnight. We are at the start of an economic transformation that will probably take 60 years to put right," he added.
